items.readable_text:
Content:
Some substances emit radiation, meaning that they release energy, often in the form of small particles, into the surrounding environment. If a substance emits radiation, it is radioactive.

Content:
Since radioactive substances are continually losing particles to the surrounding environment, the mass of a radioactive substance will decrease over time.

Content:
The mass [MATH: M(t)] of a radioactive sample is governed by the differential equation

Content:
[MATH: M'(t) = -kM(t), \qquad M(0) = M_0,]

Content:
where [MATH: t] is the time, [MATH: M_0] is the initial mass of the sample, and the constant [MATH: k] is dependent upon the type of substance.

Content:
The general solution to this initial value problem is

Content:
[MATH: M(t) = M_0 e^{-kt}.]

Content:
A graph showing how the mass of a typical radioactive substance varies with time is shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/8bd57aa4be685413de1b9271f1ec6d76]

Content:
Every type of radioactive substance has a value of [MATH: k] associated with it. However, rather than working with [MATH: k,] physicists and chemists tend to prefer working with the half-life of a substance. The half-life of a particular substance is the time it takes for a sample of that substance to decrease by a factor of one-half.

Content:
The half-life of a substance is denoted [MATH: t_{1/2},] and is the time indicated in the diagram below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/2e7f4e2df3aea321c1398e87f9f5bcc9]

Content:
The half-life also tells us how long it takes for the mass of the substance to halve once again.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/b014930af9efe95a05ad1fa495c299cf]

Content:
And again.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/bf7deb18040eee84b151107bede68b4a]

Content:
This pattern of continually halving in mass continues indefinitely.

sections.normalized_html: The half-life of bismuth-210 is [MATH: 5.012] days. How long does it take for a [MATH: 1\,280\,\textrm g] sample of bismuth-210 to reduce to [MATH: 5\,\textrm g?]
sections.readable_text: The half-life of bismuth-210 is [MATH: 5.012] days. How long does it take for a [MATH: 1\,280\,\textrm g] sample of bismuth-210 to reduce to [MATH: 5\,\textrm g?]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The mass [MATH: M(t)] of a radioactive substance at time [MATH: t] can be modeled by the differential equation

[MATH: M'(t) = -kM(t), \qquad M(0) = M_0.]

The general solution to this equation is

[MATH: M(t) = M_0e^{-kt}.]

The half-life [MATH: t_{1/2}] is the time taken for the mass of the substance to reduce by one half and is given by

[MATH: t_{1/2} = \dfrac{\ln 2}{k}.]

There are two methods that we can use to solve this problem. We describe each of them below.

Method 1

Since we know that [MATH: t_{1/2} = 5.012] days we have

[MATH: 5.012 = \dfrac{\ln 2}{k}\quad\Rightarrow\quad k = \dfrac{\ln 2}{5.012}]

Also, since [MATH: M_0 = 1\,280\,\textrm g,] we have the particular solution

[MATH: M(t) = 1\,280 e^{-t\ln 2/5.012}.]

We wish to calculate the time [MATH: t] such that [MATH: M(t) = 5\,\textrm g.] So, we set up our equation as follows:

[MATH: 5 = 1\,280 e^{-t\ln 2/5.012}]

Solving this equation for [MATH: t,] we get

[MATH: 5|= 1280e^{− t\ln 2/5.012}; (5)/(1280)|= e^{− t\ln 2/5.012}; (1)/(256)|= e^{− t\ln 2/5.012}; \ln ((1)/(256))|= \ln (e^{− t\ln 2/5.012}); \ln 1 − \ln 256|= − (t\ln 2)/(5.012); − \ln 256|= − (t\ln 2)/(5.012); t|= (5.012 ⋅ \ln 256)/(\ln 2); t|≈ 40.]

Therefore, we conclude that it takes approximately [MATH: 40] days for the mass of the substance to reduce to [MATH: 5\,\textrm g.]

Method 2

We wish to calculate the time [MATH: t] such that [MATH: M(t) = 5\,\textrm g.] Notice that

[MATH: (M(t))/(M(0))|= (5g)/(1280g); = (1)/(256); = ((1)/(2))^{8},]

or equivalently

[MATH: M(t) = \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^8\cdot M(0).]

From this equation, we see that [MATH: 8] half-lives must have occurred for the mass to reduce from [MATH: 1\,280\,\textrm g] to [MATH: 5\,\textrm g.] Hence,

[MATH: t = 8\cdot t_{1/2} =8 \cdot 5.012 \approx 40.]

Therefore, we conclude that it takes approximately [MATH: 40] days for the mass of the substance to reduce to [MATH: 5\,\textrm g.]

sections.normalized_html:
The mass [MATH: M(t)] of a radioactive substance at time [MATH: t] can be modeled by the differential equation

[MATH: M'(t) = -kM(t), \qquad M(0) = M_0.]

The general solution to this equation is

[MATH: M(t) = M_0e^{-kt}.]

The half-life [MATH: t_{1/2}] is the time taken for the mass of the substance to reduce by one half and is given by

[MATH: t_{1/2} = \dfrac{\ln 2}{k}.]

Since we know that [MATH: t_{1/2} = 301] thousand years, we have

[MATH: 301 = \dfrac{\ln 2}{k}\quad\Rightarrow\quad k = \dfrac{\ln 2}{301}.]

So, we have [MATH: M(t) = M_0 e^{-t\ln 2/301}.]

We wish to calculate the time [MATH: t] such that [MATH: M(t) = 0.65 M_0.] So, we set up our equation as follows:

[MATH: 0.65M_0 = M_0 e^{-t\ln 2/301}]

Solving this equation for [MATH: t,] we get

[MATH: 0.65M_{0}|= M_{0}e^{− t\ln 2/301}; 0.65M_{0}|= M_{0}e^{− t\ln 2/301}; 0.65|= e^{− t\ln 2/301}; \ln (0.65)|= \ln (e^{− t\ln 2/301}); \ln (0.65)|= − (t\ln 2)/(301); t|= − (301 ⋅ \ln (0.65))/(\ln 2); t|≈ 187.]

Therefore, we conclude that the object is approximately [MATH: 187] thousand years old.

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Some substances emit radiation, meaning that they release energy, often in the form of small particles, into the surrounding environment. If a substance emits radiation, it is radioactive.

Content:
Since radioactive substances are continually losing particles to the surrounding environment, the mass of a radioactive substance will decrease over time.

Content:
The mass [MATH: M(t)] of a radioactive sample is governed by the differential equation

Content:
[MATH: M'(t) = -kM(t), \qquad M(0) = M_0,]

Content:
where [MATH: t] is the time, [MATH: M_0] is the initial mass of the sample, and the constant [MATH: k] is dependent upon the type of substance.

Content:
The general solution to this initial value problem is

Content:
[MATH: M(t) = M_0 e^{-kt}.]

Content:
A graph showing how the mass of a typical radioactive substance varies with time is shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/8bd57aa4be685413de1b9271f1ec6d76]

Content:
Every type of radioactive substance has a value of [MATH: k] associated with it. However, rather than working with [MATH: k,] physicists and chemists tend to prefer working with the half-life of a substance. The half-life of a particular substance is the time it takes for a sample of that substance to decrease by a factor of one-half.

Content:
The half-life of a substance is denoted [MATH: t_{1/2},] and is the time indicated in the diagram below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/2e7f4e2df3aea321c1398e87f9f5bcc9]

Content:
The half-life also tells us how long it takes for the mass of the substance to halve once again.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/b014930af9efe95a05ad1fa495c299cf]

Content:
And again.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/bf7deb18040eee84b151107bede68b4a]

Content:
This pattern of continually halving in mass continues indefinitely.

---

Item 2 — Tutorial: Deriving a Formula for the Half-Life

Content:
The mass [MATH: M(t)] of a radioactive substance is given by

Content:
[MATH: M(t) = M_0 e^{-kt}.]

Content:
The half-life of a substance is the time taken for the mass of a sample to reduce by a factor of one-half. Therefore, it is the solution to the equation

Content:
[MATH: \dfrac12 M_0 = M_0 e^{-kt}.]

Content:
We can solve this equation for [MATH: t,] as follows:

Content:
[MATH: (1)/(2)M_{0}|= M_{0}e^{− kt}; (1)/(2)M_{0}|= M_{0}e^{− kt}; (1)/(2)|= e^{− kt}; \ln ((1)/(2))|= \ln (e^{− kt}); \ln 1 − \ln 2|= − kt; − \ln 2|= − kt; t|= (\ln 2)/(k).]

Content:
Therefore, the half-life of a substance is given by the formula

Content:
[MATH: t_{1/2} = \dfrac{\ln 2}{k}.]

Content:
Every radioactive substance has a half-life associated with it. It depends only on the substance itself and is independent of its initial mass of the sample (we know this because we were able to cancel [MATH: M_0] in our derivation of [MATH: t_{1/2}]).

Content:
It's worth noting that half-lives show significant variation in magnitude across different substances. Some substances that decay very rapidly have half-lives on the order of nanoseconds. On the other hand, some substances that decay very slowly have half-lives that are on the order of billions of years.

---

Item 3 — Example: Using the Half-Life Formula

Example Prompt:
The mass [MATH: M(t),] in grams, of a sample of iron-60 is given by

[MATH: M(t) = 100 e^{-kt},]

where [MATH: t] is the time, in millions of years. The half-life of iron-60 is [MATH: 2.6] million years. Rounded to three significant figures, what is the value of [MATH: k?]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The mass [MATH: M(t)] of a radioactive substance at time [MATH: t] can be modeled by the differential equation

[MATH: M'(t) = -kM(t), \qquad M(0) = M_0.]

The general solution to this equation is

[MATH: M(t) = M_0e^{-kt}.]

The half-life [MATH: t_{1/2}] is the time taken for the mass of the substance to reduce by one half and is given by

[MATH: t_{1/2} = \dfrac{\ln 2}{k}.]

Since we know that [MATH: t_{1/2} = 2.6] million years, we have

[MATH: 2.6 = \dfrac{\ln 2}{k}\quad\Rightarrow\quad k = \dfrac{\ln 2}{2.6} \approx 0.267.]

---

Item 6 — Example: Solving Problems Involving Radioactive Decay Given the Half-Life of a Substance

Example Prompt:
The half-life of bismuth-210 is [MATH: 5.012] days. How long does it take for a [MATH: 1\,280\,\textrm g] sample of bismuth-210 to reduce to [MATH: 5\,\textrm g?]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The mass [MATH: M(t)] of a radioactive substance at time [MATH: t] can be modeled by the differential equation

[MATH: M'(t) = -kM(t), \qquad M(0) = M_0.]

The general solution to this equation is

[MATH: M(t) = M_0e^{-kt}.]

The half-life [MATH: t_{1/2}] is the time taken for the mass of the substance to reduce by one half and is given by

[MATH: t_{1/2} = \dfrac{\ln 2}{k}.]

There are two methods that we can use to solve this problem. We describe each of them below.

Method 1

Since we know that [MATH: t_{1/2} = 5.012] days we have

[MATH: 5.012 = \dfrac{\ln 2}{k}\quad\Rightarrow\quad k = \dfrac{\ln 2}{5.012}]

Also, since [MATH: M_0 = 1\,280\,\textrm g,] we have the particular solution

[MATH: M(t) = 1\,280 e^{-t\ln 2/5.012}.]

We wish to calculate the time [MATH: t] such that [MATH: M(t) = 5\,\textrm g.] So, we set up our equation as follows:

[MATH: 5 = 1\,280 e^{-t\ln 2/5.012}]

Solving this equation for [MATH: t,] we get

[MATH: 5|= 1280e^{− t\ln 2/5.012}; (5)/(1280)|= e^{− t\ln 2/5.012}; (1)/(256)|= e^{− t\ln 2/5.012}; \ln ((1)/(256))|= \ln (e^{− t\ln 2/5.012}); \ln 1 − \ln 256|= − (t\ln 2)/(5.012); − \ln 256|= − (t\ln 2)/(5.012); t|= (5.012 ⋅ \ln 256)/(\ln 2); t|≈ 40.]

Therefore, we conclude that it takes approximately [MATH: 40] days for the mass of the substance to reduce to [MATH: 5\,\textrm g.]

Method 2

We wish to calculate the time [MATH: t] such that [MATH: M(t) = 5\,\textrm g.] Notice that

[MATH: (M(t))/(M(0))|= (5g)/(1280g); = (1)/(256); = ((1)/(2))^{8},]

or equivalently

[MATH: M(t) = \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right)^8\cdot M(0).]

From this equation, we see that [MATH: 8] half-lives must have occurred for the mass to reduce from [MATH: 1\,280\,\textrm g] to [MATH: 5\,\textrm g.] Hence,

[MATH: t = 8\cdot t_{1/2} =8 \cdot 5.012 \approx 40.]

Therefore, we conclude that it takes approximately [MATH: 40] days for the mass of the substance to reduce to [MATH: 5\,\textrm g.]

---
